passages: Adam Smith explained that a society becomes richer when people specialize in one task. In his famous example, a small factory that makes pins can produce thousands of pins a day if each worker handles only one step. If each worker had to make a whole pin alone, the total would be tiny. Smith believed that this division of labor, together with free exchange between people, raises productivity and improves the standard of living for ordinary families.

John Stuart Mill asked a simple but difficult question: when may a society control an individual? He answered that the only good reason is to prevent harm to other people. A person's own good, whether physical or moral, is not enough. Mill also feared the pressure of public opinion, which he called a kind of tyranny, because it can silence unusual ideas even when the law allows them.

Thomas Hobbes lived through a civil war, and this shaped his view of human nature. He imagined a world with no government, which he called the state of nature, and argued that fear and competition would lead to constant conflict. To escape this danger, people agree to give up some freedom and obey a strong sovereign. For Hobbes, security is the first duty of any state, and without it other freedoms have little value.

Machiavelli wrote for rulers who needed to survive in a dangerous political world. He argued that a leader must understand reality as it is, not as it should be. This approach is often called realism. A ruler who relies only on good intentions may lose power to others who are willing to act with force or cunning. Critics say this view excuses cruelty, while supporters say it simply describes how power works.

Clausewitz taught that war cannot be understood as a pure science. Information is incomplete, plans fail, and small events can change the result. He used the word friction for all the little difficulties that make real war harder than war on paper. Above all, he insisted that war serves a political purpose, so any military action should be judged by the goal it is supposed to achieve.

The authors of The Federalist Papers worried that anyone who holds too much power will eventually abuse it. Their solution was to divide government into separate branches, each able to limit the others. This system, known as checks and balances, does not assume that officials are bad people. It assumes that ambition is natural and must be controlled by the design of institutions.

Marcus Aurelius was an emperor, yet his private notes are about self-discipline, not power. He reminded himself to focus on his own thoughts and actions, because outside events are often beyond control. This idea is central to Stoicism. A calm mind, he believed, does not fight the unavoidable but responds with reason and duty.

In 1904, Halford Mackinder argued that geography shapes the fate of nations. He believed that the vast inland area of Eurasia, which he called the pivot area or Heartland, was hard for sea powers to reach and rich in resources. A state that controlled it, he warned, could gain enormous strength. Later scholars disagreed about how true this is, but his ideas still influence debates on great-power competition.
